title: Directed Energy Metal Sintering Arrays: Precision Fabrication at the Corporate Tier
body:
Directed Energy Metal Sintering Arrays (DEMSAs) are high-capital additive manufacturing systems that use precisely controlled laser or electron beam energy to fuse successive layers of metal powder—titanium alloys, hardened steels, nickel superalloys, copper composites—into dense, near-net-shape components with mechanical properties approaching or exceeding those of wrought stock. A DEMSA build chamber operates under inert atmosphere or hard vacuum to prevent oxidation during fusion, and the powder handling systems that feed the chamber are themselves precision instruments requiring regular maintenance and calibration. Build times range from hours to days depending on component complexity, and post-processing—stress relief heat treatment, surface finishing, dimensional verification—adds further lead time. The technology is not fast, but it produces geometries that no subtractive process can achieve: internal lattice structures, conformal cooling channels, gradient material compositions.

DEMSAs in GLMZ are almost exclusively corporate-tier assets. The capital cost of a production-grade array—typically in the range of several million credits—combined with the facility requirements (vibration isolation, atmospheric control, powder handling infrastructure, post-processing equipment) places them firmly within the manufacturing divisions of major corporations and their Tier-1 contractor suppliers. These firms use DEMSAs to produce high-value components for aerospace systems, medical implants, advanced weapons platforms, and critical infrastructure hardware where performance tolerances cannot be met by conventional manufacturing. The systems run under strict digital rights management: build files are encrypted, component geometries are watermarked at the microstructural level during sintering, and completed parts carry embedded provenance data readable by corporate quality systems.

The watermarking of DEMSA-produced components has become a significant dimension of GLMZ's black market economy. Counterfeit medical implants, weapon components, and structural hardware produced on unlicensed or modified DEMSA-derivative systems lack the embedded provenance markers that corporate supply chains require—but also lack the quality controls that make legitimate DEMSA output reliable. Underground DEMSA operators, working with salvaged or reverse-engineered systems in the deeper industrial zones, produce components that are visually and dimensionally indistinguishable from legitimate output but may have subtle porosity defects, incorrect alloy composition, or residual stress patterns that cause premature failure. The market for counterfeit DEMSA output is substantial and growing, driven by the difficulty and expense of accessing legitimate corporate supply chains for critical components.

At the intersection of DEMSA technology and GLMZ's augmentation economy, the production of custom biocompatible implant components occupies a particularly fraught space. Legitimate medical DEMSA production is tightly regulated, with material purity standards, sterility protocols, and biocompatibility certification requirements that add significant cost and lead time. Underground medical fabricators—sometimes called 'chop shops' in pejorative corporate media framing, 'body engineers' in the communities they serve—operate DEMSA-derivative systems to produce custom implant components for clients who cannot access or afford the corporate medical tier. The quality of this output varies enormously with operator skill and equipment condition, and the absence of post-market surveillance means failures often go untracked.
headings: Provenance Watermarking and the Counterfeit Component Market
